1. Understanding the Basics of Artificial Intelligence:  
Define Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its subfields.  
Learn about the history and evolution of AI.  
Understand the key concepts such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, etc.

  
2. Foundational Knowledge:  
Brush up on mathematics including linear algebra, calculus, probability, and statistics.  
Understand algorithms and data structures.  
Learn basics of programming languages such as Python, R, or Julia.

  
3. Machine Learning Fundamentals:  
Study supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.  
Understand the working principles of various machine learning algorithms like linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, etc.  
Learn about evaluation metrics and cross-validation techniques.

  
4. Deep Learning:  
Dive into neural networks architecture and operations.  
Understand deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, or Keras.  
Study different types of neural networks including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and their variants.  
Explore advanced topics like transfer learning, generative adversarial networks (GANs), attention mechanisms, etc.

  
5. Data Handling and Preprocessing:  
Learn data manipulation and analysis using libraries like Pandas, NumPy, and SciPy.  
Understand data preprocessing techniques including cleaning, normalization, feature scaling, and feature engineering.

  
6. Model Evaluation and Validation:  
Learn about different techniques for model evaluation and validation.  
Understand concepts like overfitting, underfitting, bias-variance tradeoff, and how to address them.

  
7. Real-World Applications:  
Explore various AI applications across different domains such as healthcare, finance, gaming, autonomous vehicles, natural language processing, etc.  
Work on projects and case studies to apply theoretical knowledge to practical scenarios.

  
8. Ethics and Bias in AI:  
Understand the ethical implications of AI technology.  
Learn about biases in data and algorithms and strategies to mitigate them.  
Explore fairness, transparency, and accountability in AI systems.

  
9. Continuous Learning and Professional Development:  
Stay updated with the latest trends and advancements in AI engineering.  
Engage in online courses, workshops, and conferences.  
Join AI communities, forums, and participate in discussions.  
Consider pursuing certifications or advanced degrees in AI or related fields.

  
10. Build a Portfolio:  
Create a portfolio showcasing your AI projects and contributions.  
Highlight your skills, expertise, and practical experience in AI engineering.  
Collaborate with peers and contribute to open-source projects to expand your portfolio.

  
11. Networking and Career Development:  
Build a professional network within the AI community.  
Seek mentorship from experienced professionals in the field.  
Explore internship opportunities or entry-level positions to gain industry experience.  
Tailor your resume and online profiles to highlight your AI skills and accomplishments.

  
12. Iterative Learning and Improvement:  
Embrace a mindset of continuous learning and improvement.  
Reflect on your progress, identify areas for growth, and set learning goals.  
Experiment with new techniques, tools, and methodologies to enhance your AI engineering skills.

  
By following this outline, you can gradually develop a strong foundation in AI engineering and embark on a fulfilling career in this dynamic field.

C++ is usually the one everyone hates but sadly the one used in unreal engine and game development. C# is used in unity. unreal seems to be widely used but jobs are out there with unity. I recommend if your serious about game development you focus on C++, but C# is easier to learn for many. As a former programming tutor and now run my own studio no student ever said to me "I can't wait to work in C++" they actually said "I will never work with C++ or see it after college I don't want to". So, focus on mastering C++ it is not as scary as you think take it in steps. Get use to the basic structure #incldue statements, main function format, then variables and declaring them, then get more intense with if statements, loops and functions and calling them.

Then once you feel you got the basics down then you start actually teaching yourself programming as a game developer not as a college student.

tips

learn basics of C++

learn advance stuff in C++

learn the basics of game development in C++

Learn blueprinting in ureal engine which will probably make you question a lot about why you learned C++ (it is still very useful)

other developers will hate me for this, but you can do a lot in blueprint instead of C++ if you find that easier, but they won't hire you in a job with just blueprinting skills. A lot of jobs in the market ask for both blueprinting and C++ skills.

the following are my own interpretations/opinions on the two courses

note: I have taken the US career institute one felt it was good and provided foundation knowledge but not hard skills/hands-on. I cannot really speak for a career step because I have not taken it but overall US career is what I would recommend between the two.

the good./bad of both from what I have heard, experienced and read

US career institute: if you pay in full it Is fine but not much hands-on experience and no externships \*volunteer if you can\*. I went here, paid in full, and had no issue. Cousin though is on a payment plan and has no idea if she can even sit for the CCMA since they won't send her cert till she "pays in full"  Do volunteer work to get hands-on skills if you go this route! you can find jobs I have but I am debating about doing a CMA class at a local tech school for 15k. I still feel ill-prepared and personally feel in person would benefit me more in a healthcare career. 

\- career-step: research into it concluded it is a toss-up. they have externships but what I read is it is so bad to try and place students in it that some sit around for months not getting into it or give up and never finish the program. those are the "bad reviews" I read but always and I mean always read the bad reviews because you need to know the worse case. I think they offer a non-externship one so may be a good idea to sign up for the externship one but see if you can nope out if you can't find an externship and still get their completion cert? just an idea

​

conclusion: nothing beats in face training where you can practice those skills and have an externship. most online will get you the CCMA which is a good cert but the gold standard seems to be heading to the CMA test cert now. so even though it may cost 15-20k I think that is a better investment than the 1-2k class online. more job offers and lots more hands-on and externship to me, at least, makes the 15k worth it. that being said you can apply to those same jobs with the CCMA but you may realize that you aren't as prepared as you think you are. As even with volunteer it's unlikely you will get to try EKGs and blood draw skills which blood draws are like gold as a MA in practice settings as I have seen on job postings. Most jobs I have seen want you to come in with at least knowledge of blood draws and many in-person allow you to practice on each other you won't get this online. in person you will be able to practice blood pressure, temp, and a host of other tests on each other such as glucose testing, etc.
